extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of American government / general readers interested in U.S. political institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria on (1) what qualities and external considerations influence the choice of a U.S. presidential candidate and why 'great men' are often not chosen, and (2) how the U.S. Cabinet is constituted and how ministers differ from European counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal qualities required in a President
rubrics_metrics.description: Firmness, common sense, and above all honesty — an honesty above all suspicion of personal interest — together with the ability to choose good subordinates and take a sound practical view of administrative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Four-fifths of a President's work is like that of a commercial chairman or railway manager: selecting competent subordinates, ensuring they attend to their business, and making practical administrative decisions. These personal merits are the chief qualities the country needs in its first magistrate in ordinary times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of sectional and State support
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief consideration in selecting a candidate is the amount of support which can be secured from different States or from different 'sections' of the Union; State feeling and sectional feeling are powerful factors in a presidential election.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The most populous sections (e.g., the Middle West and Northwest) count for most; a man from the section or State that identifies with particular interests has prima facie advantage. Party strategists value where electoral votes can be secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of being from a large State
rubrics_metrics.description: A large State casts a heavier vote in the election and is more likely to carry one of its own children than a stranger; ceteris paribus, a man from a large State is preferable as a candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fellow-citizens feel honoured and gain material advantage (favours the administration can bestow), so state-origin affects electability and strategic calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for candidates from 'doubtful' states
rubrics_metrics.description: Ceteris paribus, a candidate from a doubtful State (one not already safe for a party) is to be preferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because some States are already safe for one party, parties prefer candidates from swing/doubtful states (e.g., New York, Indiana historically) to maximize chances of winning key electoral votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious belief or declared disbelief as a disqualifying factor (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, a Roman Catholic or an avowed disbeliever in Christianity would be an undesirable candidate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is given as an example of minor disqualifying circumstances that have affected nominations in past periods; reflects historical sectarian and cultural biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Military service as an electoral advantage (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who had fought, especially with distinction in the Northern army after the Civil War, enjoyed great advantages in presidential contests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: General Grant's two elections show the weight of military service as a consideration; soldiers rallied to such names, making military record a potent electoral asset in that era.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past greatness can hinder later political return
rubrics_metrics.description: Past greatness is often an encumbrance rather than a help to resuming a political career; exalted power exposes weaknesses and creates enemies, and a former President may be regarded as having had his day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Few ex-Presidents play a part in politics after leaving office; practical barriers (lack of vacancies, dislike of campaigning) and reputational exposure during tenure reduce prospects of political comeback.

rubrics_metrics.name: When great personal qualities prevail
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual ability and strength of character can influence the choice of a candidate and may be decisive, particularly when times are critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These qualities naturally count most in crises; reform movements claim their weight will rise as public disgust with professional politicians grows. Historical examples show that in some periods greatmen (e.g., Lincoln, Grant) did attain the presidency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasons great men are not often chosen
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men are not often chosen as Presidents because (1) great men are rare in politics, (2) the method of choice may not bring them to the top, and (3) in quiet times they are not absolutely needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author summarizes structural and situational impediments (rarity, selection methods, absence of necessity) to the election of 'great' Presidents, and notes historical periods with differing quality of presidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet appointments: Presidential choice with Senate consent and presidential removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Cabinet officers are appointed by the President, subject to the consent of the Senate (practically never refused), and may be removed by the President alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nothing marks them off from other department heads except that they are summoned to the President's private council; historically the President often forms a new cabinet on entering office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional restriction on ministers holding Congressional seats
rubrics_metrics.description: No person holding any office under the United States shall be a member of either House during his continuance in office (Art. XI §6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was intended to prevent the President from corrupting representatives via officeholders; ministers therefore do not sit in Congress or vote, though the Constitution is silent about addressing the Houses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers are the President's servants, not a collectively responsible cabinet
rubrics_metrics.description: American ministers are individually dependent on and answerable to the President, with no joint policy and no collective responsibility; the Administration does not work as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike parliamentary systems, ministers are not accountable to the legislature as a body, do not form a committee of the legislature, and adverse votes in Congress do not compel resignation. Meetings of ministers serve consultation, not collective government-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wide Presidential latitude in selecting ministers (including outsiders)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President has the amplest range of choice: he can appoint men who have never sat in Congress or even in politics; generally, appointees have at least local importance and often are those to whom the President owes his election or leaders/competitors in the party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lincoln appointing Seward and Chase (his nearest competitors) to major cabinet posts; cabinets often balance party factions, reward supporters, or secure backing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and stature of the Secretary of State
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of State is the most dignified place in the cabinet and often given to a leader of the party; conduct of foreign affairs is the chief duty and the Secretary often has a larger stage and more chances of fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The State Secretary practically shapes the administration's foreign policy except as controlled by the Senate; the department keeps archives, publishes statutes, and oversees diplomatic/consular services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of the Treasury as minister of finance (limited compared to Europe)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Treasury is the minister of finance but lacks the same range as a European finance minister because he is excluded from Congress and has little direct role in taxation or appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically important at founding and wartime for managing loans/currency; today handles currency and national debt management within Congressional limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of the Interior's U.S.-specific role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of the Interior is not as omnipresent a minister as in Europe; chiefly occupied with public lands, Indian affairs, patents, pensions, the meteorological office, geological survey, and reclamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many functions handled by states elsewhere; department responsibilities reflect U.S. federal structure and territorial concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney-General's functions and political nature of appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: The Attorney-General is public prosecutor, standing counsel for the United States, and to some extent a minister of justice with oversight of federal judicial departments; his opinions may be authoritative for executive officials and he controls prosecutions under federal acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often a lawyer of eminence, but political considerations heavily influence the President's choice; published opinions justify executive conduct and indicate legal views on executive powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of executive departments reflects growth of government functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Creation of Departments of Commerce and Labour evidences extension of government functions into new fields; Commerce supervises interstate corporations (other than railroads), lighthouses, coasts surveys, merchant shipping, census, trade statistics; Labour administers immigration laws, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The departmental list shows areas handled at federal level; absence of certain ministries (education, worship, public works) stems from federalism and Congressional primacy for some public works appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences from European parliamentary cabinets: principles not holding in U.S.
rubrics_metrics.description: Four parliamentary principles (irresponsible head of state with responsible cabinet; ministers sit in legislature; ministers accountable to legislature and must resign when losing confidence; collective ministerial liability) do not hold in America.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S. the President is personally responsible to the people, ministers do not sit in Congress or form a legislature-chosen committee, they are not accountable to Congress, and responsibility is not collective but individual to the President; deadlocks between President and Congress are an accepted constitutional consequence.
